name: The Causeway Collective
motto: Nobody else was going to do it.
description:
The Causeway Collective started as a neighborhood watch in Milwaukee's Kinnickinnic corridor and became something more out of pure necessity. When climate refugees began flooding into the Great Lakes zone in the 2070s, Milwaukee's lower wards absorbed tens of thousands of displaced people with zero institutional support. The corporate governance structure had no incentive to help people who couldn't pay taxes or buy products. So the residents — a mix of long-term locals and earlier waves of refugees — organized their own defense, their own food distribution, their own dispute resolution. The Causeway Collective is what that organization became.

They're about 180 strong, which makes them one of the larger street-level groups, but their numbers are misleading. Only about forty are active fighters. The rest are medics, logistics coordinators, food growers, and community organizers who make the neighborhood function. The Collective runs three community kitchens, maintains a water purification system cobbled together from salvaged parts, and operates a rotating patrol that keeps the worst predators out of their blocks. They're not a gang in the traditional sense — they don't sell drugs, don't run protection rackets, and don't engage in organized crime. They're a militia that formed because the alternative was letting their neighbors starve or be preyed upon.

The complication is funding. Running a parallel social infrastructure costs money that idealism doesn't generate. The Collective funds itself through a combination of community contributions, barter arrangements, and — increasingly — contract work that blurs the line between community defense and mercenary activity. Collective fighters hire out as security for convoys, guard duty for businesses in adjacent neighborhoods, and occasionally as muscle for operations they'd rather not discuss at community meetings.
ideology: Mutual aid as survival strategy. The Collective believes that corporate governance has abandoned the lower wards and that community self-organization is the only viable response. They're not revolutionaries — they're pragmatists who'd happily disband if legitimate services existed. They don't.
territory: Milwaukee's Kinnickinnic corridor and surrounding lower wards, roughly twelve square blocks of residential and light commercial space.
methods: Community patrol — rotating armed patrols that maintain a visible security presence
Food distribution — three community kitchens serving hundreds of daily meals from urban farms and scavenged supplies
Water purification — a jury-rigged filtration system serving the corridor's residents
Dispute arbitration — a council of community elders who resolve conflicts before they escalate
Contract security — hiring out fighters for external work to fund internal operations
Refugee integration — processing and housing new arrivals, maintaining census records the city doesn't keep
resources: 180 members with a strong sense of community obligation
Three community kitchens and a water purification system
An armory of scavenged and purchased weapons — nothing military-grade, but functional
Detailed knowledge of the lower wards' infrastructure, population, and vulnerabilities
Community trust — the Collective is one of the few organizations that residents genuinely support
Experienced fighters hardened by years of neighborhood defense

relationships.name: The Fathom Line
relationships.reason: Milwaukee's water routes are finite; the Collective and the Line dispute access to several key corridors

relationships.name: The Shore Dogs
relationships.reason: Coastal distribution conflicts with the Shore Dogs' Great Lakes operation at several handoff points

relationships.name: The Interchange
relationships.reason: The Collective feeds Milwaukee commerce into the Interchange's GLMZ-wide distribution network

relationships.name: The Last Mile
relationships.reason: The Last Mile delivers what the Collective moves; operational partnership in the Milwaukee-Chicago corridor

story_hooks: The Collective needs a freelancer for a job too dirty for their community reputation — but the pay funds the kitchens
A corporate developer wants the Kinnickinnic corridor and is pressuring the Collective to dissolve — or be dissolved
A Collective council member is secretly diverting funds, and exposing them would fracture the community
New refugees are arriving with skills — and secrets — that multiple factions want access to
The Collective's water system is failing and the parts to fix it are in territory controlled by a hostile gang
